name: Snowy Mountain
description: There are $$$n$$$ locations on a snowy mountain range (numbered from $$$1$$$ to $$$n$$$), connected by $$$n-1$$$ trails in the shape of a tree. Each trail has length $$$1$$$. Some of the locations are base lodges. The height $$$h_i$$$ of each location is equal to the distance to the nearest base lodge (a base lodge has height $$$0$$$). There is a skier at each location, each skier has initial kinetic energy $$$0$$$. Each skier wants to ski along as many trails as possible. Suppose that the skier is skiing along a trail from location $$$i$$$ to $$$j$$$. Skiers are not allowed to ski uphill (i.e., if $$$h_i \lt h_j$$$). It costs one unit of kinetic energy to ski along flat ground (i.e., if $$$h_i = h_j$$$), and a skier gains one unit of kinetic energy by skiing downhill (i.e., if $$$h_i \gt h_j$$$). For each location, compute the length of the longest sequence of trails that the skier starting at that location can ski along without their kinetic energy ever becoming negative. Skiers are allowed to visit the same location or trail multiple times.
input_specification: The first line contains a single integer $$$n$$$ ($$$2 \le n \le 2 \cdot 10^5$$$). The second line contains $$$n$$$ integers $$$l_1, l_2, \ldots, l_n$$$ ($$$0 \le l_i \le 1$$$). If $$$l_i = 1$$$, location $$$i$$$ is a base lodge; if $$$l_i = 0$$$, location $$$i$$$ is not a base lodge. It is guaranteed that there is at least $$$1$$$ base lodge. Each of the next $$$n-1$$$ lines contains two integers $$$u, v$$$ ($$$1 \leq u, v \leq n$$$, $$$u \neq v$$$), meaning that there is a trail that connects the locations $$$u$$$ and $$$v$$$. It is guaranteed that the given trails form a tree.
output_specification: Print $$$n$$$ integers: the $$$i$$$-th integer is equal to the length of the longest sequence of trails that the skier starting at location $$$i$$$ can ski along without their kinetic energy ever becoming negative.
approach_summary: Formulate the state transition graph with non-negative weights. Execute Dijkstra's algorithm with priority queue to find shortest paths in O((V + E) log V).

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 1654G — Snowy Mountain [168. Dijkstra's Algorithm]
topic_editorial.summary: Single-source shortest path using Dijkstra's algorithm.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: Because all edge weights are non-negative, the shortest distance to the unvisited vertex with the minimum tentative distance is finalized and cannot be decreased by further transitions (greedy choice property).
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Graph Modeling
Construct an adjacency list with pairs $(v, w)$ for each directed or undirected edge from $u$ to $v$ with weight $w \ge 0$.

### Step 2: Distance Table Initialization
Initialize $dist[v] = \infty$ for all vertices, with $dist[\text{source}] = 0$.
Push $(0, \text{source})$ into a min-priority queue `std::priority_queue<pair<long long, int>, vector<pair<long long, int>>, greater<>>`.

### Step 3: Relaxation Loop
While the priority queue is not empty:
1. Pop $(d, u)$. If $d > dist[u]$, discard (stale entry).
2. For each neighbor $(v, w)$ of $u$:
   If $dist[u] + w < dist[v]$:
   $$dist[v] = dist[u] + w$$
   Push $(dist[v], v)$ into the priority queue.
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}((V + E) \log V)$
  Every vertex is extracted from the priority queue at most once. For every edge, we perform at most one priority queue push operation taking $\mathcal{O}(\log V)$.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(V + E)$
  Required for storing the adjacency list and the distance array.
